name: Microprocessor and Computer Architecture
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance). Confirm the split in your college's notice.

units.title: Microprocessors and the Intel 8085
topics: A microprocessor system and its buses
Seeing the ideas: real chips, buses, multiplexing, timing and flags

sections.title: A microprocessor system and its buses
Seeing the ideas: real chips, buses, multiplexing, timing and flags

summary: A microprocessor is a CPU on a chip; a system joins CPU, memory and I/O with address, data and control buses.
The 8085 has an accumulator, six general registers (pairs BC, DE, HL; M = byte at HL), PC, SP and five flags S, Z, AC, P, CY.
AD0–AD7 are multiplexed; ALE and a latch separate the low address byte from the data.
An instruction cycle consists of machine cycles (opcode fetch plus reads/writes), each of 3–6 T-states.
Five hardware interrupts with fixed priority and eight software RSTs.
The 8086 adds a wider bus, a prefetch queue (BIU/EU), segmentation and hardware multiply/divide.

units.title: 8085 Instruction Set and Assembly Programming
topics: Seeing the ideas: opcodes, addressing modes, loops, delays and the stack

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: opcodes, addressing modes, loops, delays and the stack

summary: Instructions are 1–3 bytes; five addressing modes: immediate, register, direct, register-indirect, implied.
Instruction groups: data transfer, arithmetic, logical/compare/rotate, branching, stack/I/O/machine control.
Typical programs follow initialise → loop (process, advance pointer, count) → store → HLT; M with HL walks arrays.
Delay loops use known T-states; one loop gives 14n + 4 T.
The stack is LIFO in RAM; CALL/RET use it for return addresses.
I/O may be memory-mapped or I/O-mapped; decoders create chip selects; the 8255 gives three programmable parallel ports.

units.title: Basic Computer Architecture
topics: Architecture, organisation and a little history
The registers of the basic computer
The instruction set of the basic computer
Seeing the ideas: stored programs, buses, instruction cycle and interrupts

sections.title: Architecture, organisation and a little history
The registers of the basic computer
The instruction set of the basic computer
Seeing the ideas: stored programs, buses, instruction cycle and interrupts

summary: Architecture is what the programmer sees; organisation is how it is built. The von Neumann machine stores program and data together; the memory hierarchy exploits locality.
The basic computer has AR, PC, DR, AC, IR, TR, INPR, OUTR, a 16-bit common bus and a ripple of load/increment/clear controls.
Instructions are I + 3-bit opcode + 12-bit address; seven memory-reference, twelve register-reference and six I/O instructions.
The control unit derives timing T0–T15 from a sequence counter and D0–D7 from the opcode.
Fetch takes T0–T2, indirect addressing adds a read, and each instruction clears SC when done; an interrupt replaces fetch with the three-step interrupt cycle.

units.title: Microprogrammed and Hardwired Control
topics: Control of the AC register and the ALU
Seeing the ideas: control units, microinstructions and real control words

sections.title: Control of the AC register and the ALU
Seeing the ideas: control units, microinstructions and real control words

summary: A micro-operation is one register-level action; a microinstruction packs those of one clock period plus the next-address information; a microprogram is the routine for one machine instruction.
Hardwired control uses gates, is fast and hard to change; microprogrammed control uses a control memory, is flexible and slower.
The sequencer chooses the next address by increment, jump, conditional jump, opcode mapping, or subroutine return.
Mano's 20-bit microinstruction has three micro-operation fields, a condition field, a branch field and a 7-bit address.
FETCH is three microinstructions, and each machine instruction's routine ends by branching back to FETCH.

units.title: Central Processing Unit and Computer Arithmetic
topics: Seeing the ideas: RISC and CISC chips, stack, addressing, Booth, floating point and division

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: RISC and CISC chips, stack, addressing, Booth, floating point and division

summary: A register-organised CPU selects ALU operands with two multiplexers and a control word SELA/SELB/SELD/OPR.
A stack gives LIFO storage, supports calls and interrupts, and evaluates postfix expressions.
Instruction formats range from three-address to zero-address; addressing modes locate operands flexibly.
Program control uses flags C, S, Z, V; subroutine calls and interrupts save the return state on the stack.
RISC: simple, fixed-length, load/store, hardwired, pipeline-friendly; CISC: complex, microprogrammed.
The ALU adds/subtracts with 2's complement, multiplies with shift-and-add or Booth, divides by restoring/non-restoring, and handles reals as IEEE 754 floating point.

units.title: Input–Output Organisation
topics: Seeing the ideas: interface chips, handshaking, serial frames, priority chain, DMA and bit stuffing

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: interface chips, handshaking, serial frames, priority chain, DMA and bit stuffing

summary: An interface adapts the peripheral to the CPU through data, status and control registers; I/O is isolated or memory-mapped.
Strobe and handshake coordinate data transfer between unsynchronised units; handshake confirms delivery.
Programmed I/O polls; interrupt-driven I/O signals; DMA moves blocks with one interrupt at the end.
Priority is resolved by software polling, daisy chain or a priority encoder; the 8259 extends the 8085's interrupt lines.
IOPs run their own channel programs; communication processors offload character- and bit-oriented protocols.

units.title: Memory Organisation
topics: Seeing the ideas: memory chips, the hierarchy, cache mapping, paging and replacement

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: memory chips, the hierarchy, cache mapping, paging and replacement

summary: The hierarchy trades size, speed and cost; locality makes it work.
SRAM for cache, DRAM for main memory, ROM family for non-volatile code; the address map and chip-select decode place chips in the address space.
A disk's access time is dominated by seek and rotation.
Caches map blocks by direct, fully associative or set-associative rules, replace by LRU/FIFO/random and write by write-through or write-back.
Virtual memory pages programs on demand; page faults are handled by the OS using FIFO/LRU-like replacement; TLBs speed translation.
Segmentation and segmented paging structure memory; base/limit registers and protection bits enforce isolation.

units.title: Pipelining, Vector Processing and Multiprocessors
topics: Seeing the ideas: assembly lines, parallel machines, hazards, branch prediction and Amdahl's law

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: assembly lines, parallel machines, hazards, branch prediction and Amdahl's law

summary: Flynn classifies computers by instruction and data streams; modern machines are mostly MIMD with SIMD units.
A k-stage pipeline gives up to k-fold speed-up, reduced by fill time, unbalanced stages and hazards.
Arithmetic pipelines segment operations like floating-point add; the four-segment instruction pipeline overlaps FI, DA, FO and EX.
Structural, data and control hazards are handled by resources, forwarding/interlocks and branch prediction.
Vector processors apply one operation to arrays, removing loop overhead; matrix multiplication is the model workload.
Multiprocessors share memory over a bus, crossbar or network; caches need coherence protocols; Amdahl's law bounds the gain.
